title: Uttara's charioteer
hook: Prince Uttara boasts he'd beat the Kuru army if only he had a charioteer, and the dance teacher volunteers
carry: parthasarathy: god holds the reins when fear comes

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bhima listened to Draupadi, then stopped Kichaka in the dancing hall. Your line was a protector's dharma: stop the cruelty.

Cattle raiders. The Kauravas have heard that Kichaka is dead, and they come for King Virata's herds. The king has already ridden out to fight raiders on another side, taking Kanka, the cook and the herdsmen with him. At home, among the women of the palace, sits his young son, Prince Uttara. And Uttara talks big. If I only had a charioteer, he says, I'd beat the whole Kuru army. They'd look at me and wonder if I was Arjuna himself. The person he's talking about is standing a few feet away, in bangles.
screen: `THE KAURAVAS RAID THE HERDS.` → `UTTARA'S BOAST.` → `ARJUNA IS IN THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Sairandhri speaks up: Brihannala once drove a chariot for Arjuna. Uttara is embarrassed, but he has no one else. The teacher fumbles the armor on purpose, and the palace women laugh. Then the chariot rolls out, and Uttara sees the army: banners, elephants, Bhishma, Drona, Karna. His boast falls apart. He jumps down and runs. Brihannala runs after him, braid flying, and some Kuru soldiers think: that runs like Arjuna. The teacher catches the prince, not to shame him but to steady him. Don't be afraid, he says, in effect. You drive. I'll fight. At the shami tree Uttara unwraps the bundle and finds the great bow Gandiva. Whose are these? And Brihannala tells him: I am Arjuna. Now hold that picture, because the epic will turn it around. Soon, on the field of Kurukshetra, Arjuna himself will lose his nerve and let his bow slip, and his charioteer, Krishna, will steady him. That conversation is the Bhagavad Gita. Many readers notice the echo: the man who says you drive, I'll fight, will soon need someone at the reins for him. It's why Hindus love Krishna as Parthasarathy, Arjuna's charioteer, and temples in his name still draw crowds. The teaching: in Hindu devotion, God doesn't only watch from far above the battle. God takes the reins beside the frightened. Today fear still makes us jump from the chariot. The epic's answer isn't shame. It's someone who runs after you.
screen: `UTTARA SEES THE ARMY, AND RUNS` · `YOU DRIVE. I'LL FIGHT.` · `KRISHNA WILL STEADY ARJUNA` · then, large: `PARTHASARATHY: GOD AT THE REINS`

segments.voice: Many Hindu homes keep a picture of Krishna driving Arjuna's chariot. Feel your feet on the floor and bring to mind one thing you've been running from. Breathing in, picture someone steady at the reins beside you: Krishna, if you pray to him, or someone who has steadied you before. Breathing out, let your hands rest, as if you could face it now, not alone. If you pray, you can bring it to God in your prayer.
Virata. The kingdom whose frightened prince learns, on a battlefield, who his dance teacher really is.
Your line: Parthasarathy: God holds the reins when fear comes. A boast, a run, and a teacher who ran after him. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Retellings of the Virata book linger on Uttara's boast and flight and on Brihannala chasing him across the field, a scene that mixes comedy with the moment Arjuna is revealed.

Uttara.meaning: King Virata's young son, who boasts and then runs

Brihannala.meaning: Arjuna's disguise: a dance teacher for the palace women

Kauravas.meaning: Duryodhana and his brothers, the Pandavas' cousins

Gandiva.meaning: Arjuna's bow, known to every warrior on sight

Bhishma.meaning: the elder of the Kuru house, a great warrior

Drona.meaning: the teacher who trained the Kuru and Pandava princes in arms

Parthasarathy.meaning: Krishna as the charioteer of Partha (Arjuna)
